strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: converting naturally occurring conversational feedback into preference-training data. The resulting 20,281-pair GPT-4 dataset and model-specific variants constitute a potentially useful contribution.

The GPT-4-data variant improves all three model families across the reported public benchmarks. AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rates increase from 24.3 to 34.9 for Phi 3, 22.9 to 34.2 for LLaMA 3, and 17.1 to 31.4 for Mistral. These results support the utility of the overall training recipe beyond the proposed evaluation.

Useful methodological details include conversation- and user-disjoint testing, evaluations with and without preference checklists, a four-annotator audit of feedback detection, and appendices specifying prompts, model versions, and core training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved alignment with actual users lacks independent validation. GPT-4 extracts feedback, summarizes preferences, generates preferred responses, and judges responses using those summaries; it also supports filtering of on-policy data. Figure 2 demonstrates that providing a checklist changes GPT-4's judgments, but does not establish that those judgments better match users. The human audit covers SAT/DSAT classification only, not summary fidelity, constructed preference pairs, or final model rankings. Independent assessment against the original feedback is needed.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of in-situ feedback. Comparisons against untuned instruction models confound feedback use with additional SFT/DPO training and GPT-4 response distillation. Table 2 compares dataset characteristics, not downstream effectiveness. A matched comparison using the same prompts and teacher without extracted preferences, alongside an established preference-data baseline, would test the claimed advantage much more directly.

The custom evaluation supports a narrower conclusion than the paper claims. Selecting the ten most mutually similar preferences within each of 70 clusters and requiring task similarity to training deliberately favors common, familiar cases; this does not establish population representativeness. Feedback-bearing conversations already cover only approximately 12.8% of the source corpus, and DSAT detection has 48.4% recall. Although selection bias is acknowledged, claims about diverse users and authentic human values remain insufficiently supported.

Some conclusions contradict the reported evidence. Section 5 claims that neither dataset variant compromises other benchmark performance, yet on-policy Mistral declines on AlpacaEval 2 LC (17.1 to 12.9), Arena-Hard (12.6 to 10.3), and MT-Bench (6.71 to 6.42). It also loses more often than it wins without checklists. Confidence intervals or training-run variability are not reported, leaving claims of significance, particularly for small improvements, unsupported.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful training details. The manuscript only promises future dataset availability and provides no accompanying artifact link. Important construction choices—including embeddings and clustering settings, precise filtering rules, split identities, and the validation criterion used for hyperparameter search—are insufficiently specified. Together with the missing independent validation and controlled comparisons, these are important revisions needed before a sound Findings recommendation; the positive benchmark results make next-cycle resubmission reasonable.
